cards.front: What are the four golden signals?
cards.back: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation — the minimum dashboard for any service. In an interview, reach for them first: ‘I’d check the four golden signals’ is the SRE equivalent of ‘let me reproduce it.’

cards.front: SLI vs SLO vs SLA?
cards.back: SLI: the measured indicator (e.g. successful requests / total). SLO: the target on the SLI (99.9% over 30 days). SLA: the contract with consequences. The interview line: ‘SLIs are facts, SLOs are promises, SLAs are contracts.’

cards.front: How do error budgets govern releases?
cards.back: Budget remaining → ship freely. Budget exhausted → freeze risky changes until reliability recovers. It replaces arguments about ‘are we reliable enough’ with arithmetic — the interview line: ‘the budget turns reliability into a joint product decision.’

cards.front: How do you explain burn-rate alerting?
cards.back: Instead of alerting on raw error counts, alert on how fast the error budget is being consumed relative to the SLO window: fast-burn (page now) vs slow-burn (ticket). Multiwindow alerts catch both without paging on blips.

cards.front: How do you measure SLIs with Prometheus?
cards.back: Counters for requests and errors (rate over windows), histograms/summaries for latency percentiles, recording rules to precompute SLI ratios, and burn-rate alert rules on top. The interview line: ‘the SLI is a PromQL expression with an SLO attached.’

quiz.q: A latency SLI in Prometheus is typically built from:
choices: Histogram buckets — enabling accurate percentile computation over windows
quiz.explain: Histograms preserve the distribution: any percentile over any window is computable.

quiz.q: Burn-rate alerting’s advantage over static error thresholds is:
choices: It measures budget consumption relative to the SLO — paging only when the objective is actually at risk
quiz.explain: Thresholds don’t know your SLO; burn rate ties paging directly to objective risk.

quiz.q: When the error budget is exhausted, the correct policy is:
choices: Freeze or slow risky releases until the budget recovers
quiz.explain: The budget is the agreed tradeoff dial: spending it all means reliability work comes first.

quiz.q: An error budget is:
choices: 1 − SLO: the allowed failure rate, spent deliberately on releases and risk
quiz.explain: 99.9% SLO → 0.1% budget: reliability as a spendable resource balancing velocity and stability.

cards.front: Walk the incident lifecycle.
cards.back: Detect (alerts, user reports) → respond (declare, assemble, IC takes command) → mitigate (stop the bleeding — rollback, shed load) → resolve → learn (blameless postmortem). The interview line: ‘mitigate first, understand second.’

cards.front: What are the incident command roles?
cards.back: Incident Commander (decides, coordinates — doesn’t debug), Communications (status updates, stakeholders), Scribe (timeline), plus subject-matter experts debugging. The IC’s job is the incident, not the keyboard.

cards.front: How do you discuss defect lifecycle and severity?
cards.back: Lifecycle: new → triaged → in progress → fixed → verified → closed (reopened if it regresses). Severity (impact) vs priority (fix order) are different axes — a cosmetic bug on the checkout button can be high priority. The interview line: ‘severity is impact; priority is scheduling.’

cards.front: How do you communicate during an outage?
cards.back: One channel (#incident), regular cadence (every 15–30 min even with ‘no update’), impact-first language (who’s affected, what we’re doing, when’s the next update), and a single comms owner. The interview line: ‘silence during an outage is a second outage.’

cards.front: What makes a postmortem blameless and useful?
cards.back: Blameless: systems and process, never people — or nobody will write honestly. Structure: timeline, impact, root causes (plural — ‘five whys’), action items with owners and dates. The interview line: ‘the postmortem’s value is the action items, not the document.’

quiz.q: An ML system design that only covers the model is weak because:
choices: Production value lives in data, serving, and monitoring — the model is one piece
quiz.explain: Most ML failures are systems failures: skew, drift, latency — not the algorithm.

quiz.q: Blameless postmortems work because:
choices: Removing blame gets honest timelines — people report what really happened
quiz.explain: Honest data requires psychological safety; blame produces cover stories instead of root causes.

quiz.q: Status updates during an outage should lead with:
choices: Customer impact: who’s affected and what’s being done
quiz.explain: Stakeholders need impact and next-update time; deep technical detail follows for those who need it.

quiz.q: Severity vs priority differ in that:
choices: Severity = impact on users; priority = order of fixing (business decision)
Severity is decided by testers only
quiz.explain: A severe bug in a deprecated feature can be low priority; a trivial bug blocking launch is high priority.

notes.body:
- **Prometheus Documentation** (https://prometheus.io/docs/) — Metrics, PromQL, and alerting references for the observability spine.
- **Grafana Documentation** (https://grafana.com/docs/) — Dashboards and alerting documentation used in the troubleshooting modules.

cards.front: Metrics, logs, traces — the three pillars in an SRE interview?
cards.back: Metrics: numbers over time (alerts, trends). Logs: discrete events with context (the why). Traces: request journeys across services (the where). The interview line: ‘metrics tell me something’s wrong, traces show me where, logs tell me why.’

cards.front: What are the four golden signals?
cards.back: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation — the minimum dashboard for any service. In an interview, reach for them first: ‘I’d check the four golden signals’ is the SRE equivalent of ‘let me reproduce it.’

cards.front: USE vs RED methods?
cards.back: USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for resources — ‘is the box healthy.’ RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) for services — ‘is the service healthy.’ In an interview, name which lens fits: debugging a host → USE; debugging an API → RED.

cards.front: Why alert on symptoms, not causes?
cards.back: Users feel symptoms (latency, error rate); causes are legion and change. Symptom alerts (burn rate, golden signals) page on user impact; cause-based alerts (‘disk 90%’) page on things that may not matter — alert fatigue follows.

cards.front: What makes a dashboard that ‘answers questions’?
cards.back: Golden signals up top, drill-down from symptom to cause, time-range comparisons, and annotations for deploys — organized by the questions on-call asks at 3am, not by data source. The interview line: ‘a dashboard is a UI for incident questions.’

quiz.q: Putting user_id in a Prometheus label is dangerous because:
choices: Each unique value creates a new time series — cardinality explosion
quiz.explain: Unbounded label values × metrics = millions of series; memory and query costs follow.

quiz.q: Deploy annotations on dashboards help because:
choices: They correlate behavior changes with releases — the first suspect in any regression
quiz.explain: ‘What changed?’ is the first incident question; annotations answer it at a glance.

quiz.q: Alerting on symptoms means paging when:
choices: User-facing indicators (latency/errors) breach SLO — regardless of underlying cause
quiz.explain: Pages should mean user impact; cause metrics are for dashboards and diagnosis, not paging.

quiz.q: The RED method suits:
quiz.explain: RED describes service behavior from the requester’s view; USE describes resource internals.

notes.body: Capacity as applied arithmetic: forecast, test, provision headroom — and narrate the cost of every extra nine.

notes.title: Sources
notes.body:
- **Google SRE Books** (https://sre.google/) — The SRE book and workbook: SLIs/SLOs, incidents, and reliability math, from the source.
- **Kubernetes Documentation** (https://kubernetes.io/docs/) — Core objects, networking, and failure-mode references for orchestration modules.

cards.front: How do you forecast demand for capacity planning?
cards.back: Historical growth rates plus known events (launches, seasonality, marketing), expressed as ranges not points, translated through the capacity model (requests → resources). The interview line: ‘forecasts are ranges with assumptions, reviewed on a cadence.’

cards.front: k6 vs JMeter — how do you compare them?
cards.back: k6: JS-scripted, developer-friendly, great for CI-integrated load tests with thresholds as gates. JMeter: GUI-driven, mature, huge protocol support, heavier. The interview line: ‘k6 for code-reviewed load tests in the pipeline; JMeter where the team already lives in it.’

cards.front: HPA vs VPA?
cards.back: HPA: more pods when load rises (horizontal — the cloud-native default). VPA: bigger pods (vertical — for workloads that can’t scale out, needs restarts). The interview caveat: autoscaling isn’t instant — cold starts and scaling lag mean you still need headroom.

cards.front: What’s the utilization wall?
cards.back: Latency degrades nonlinearly as utilization approaches 100% (queueing theory): a system at 90%+ has no headroom for bursts — the ‘wall’ where small load increases cause large latency spikes. The interview line: ‘I plan headroom against the wall, not against the average.’

cards.front: What’s the N+1 query problem and its fix?
cards.back: Loading N parents then one query per parent’s children: N+1 round trips. The fix is eager loading — a JOIN or batched second query (and ORMs have explicit eager-loading APIs). Name it when you see loops over queries.

quiz.q: Spot instances fit batch workloads because:
choices: Interruption-tolerant work buys spare capacity at deep discounts
quiz.explain: Price follows preemptibility; batch work that checkpoints doesn’t care.

quiz.q: Eager loading fixes N+1 by:
choices: Fetching related rows in bulk (JOIN or batched query) instead of one query per parent
quiz.explain: One bulk fetch replaces N per-row queries; round trips collapse from N+1 to ~2.

quiz.q: Running a service at 95% CPU is risky because:
choices: Queueing effects make latency spike nonlinearly near saturation — no burst headroom
quiz.explain: Near 100% utilization, tiny load increases produce huge queueing delays.

quiz.q: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler reacts to load by:
quiz.explain: HPA scales replica count on metrics; VPA resizes individual pods.

cards.front: How do you design for multi-region in an interview?
cards.back: Active-passive (one serves, one stands by) vs active-active (both serve — needs conflict resolution); data replication with RPO/RTO stated; DNS or anycast failover; and the honest cost: complexity and consistency tradeoffs multiply. The interview line: ‘multi-region is a business decision with an engineering price.’

cards.front: What is backpressure, and where do you put it?
cards.back: When consumers are slower than producers, pressure must go somewhere: bounded queues that block/shed, reactive streams with demand signaling, or Kafka consumer-lag alerting. The interview point: an unbounded queue is a deferred outage.

cards.front: How do caching layers behave under failure?
cards.back: Cache stampedes on cold start, thundering herd on hot-key expiry, and the deadly combo: cache down → DB overload → cascading failure. Defenses: request coalescing, staggered TTLs, circuit breakers, and graceful degradation (serve stale while revalidating).

cards.front: What’s load shedding, and when do you use it?
cards.back: Deliberately dropping low-priority work to protect the core: priority queues, shedding non-critical traffic at the edge, degrading features gracefully. The interview line: ‘shedding is a choice — uncontrolled collapse is not.’

cards.front: What’s the standard system-design walkthrough?
cards.back: Requirements → estimation → API → data model → happy-path design → scaling/bottlenecks → failure modes → tradeoffs summary. Drive with questions, think aloud, and treat the interviewer as a collaborator, not an examiner.

quiz.q: In a design round, the interviewer is best treated as:
choices: A collaborator — ask questions, incorporate feedback, design together
quiz.explain: Design rounds simulate real design work: collaborative, iterative, tradeoff-driven.

quiz.q: Load shedding differs from a cascading failure in that it’s:
choices: Deliberate and prioritized — you choose what degrades instead of everything failing
quiz.explain: Controlled degradation preserves the critical path; cascades take everything down.

quiz.q: Serving stale cache during an origin outage is:
choices: Graceful degradation — slightly old data beats no data
quiz.explain: Stale-while-revalidate as a failure mode keeps the product usable while the origin recovers.

quiz.q: A bounded queue with a drop-or-block policy implements:
choices: Backpressure — the producer feels the consumer’s slowness
quiz.explain: Bounded buffers propagate slowness upstream instead of growing memory until collapse.

cards.front: How do you prep for SRE mock rounds (incident, metrics/SLO, system design)?
cards.back: Incident: run the lifecycle aloud (declare, mitigate first, comms cadence). Metrics/SLO: define SLIs, do the budget math, name burn-rate alerting. Design: requirements → estimation → HA design → failure modes. The interview line: ‘each round has a shape — I rehearse the shape.’

cards.front: How do behavioral rounds differ for SREs?
cards.back: They probe ownership under pressure: on-call stories, incident decisions, disagreements about risk, and learning from outages — all STAR, all blameless. The interview line: ‘SRE behavioral rounds grade how I act when the pager fires.’

cards.front: How do you score yourself against an interview rubric?
cards.back: Fixed axes per round type: correctness, complexity analysis, communication, time management, tradeoffs named. Score honestly after every mock; the rubric turns feelings into data. The interview line: ‘I grade myself the way they’ll grade me.’

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?
cards.back: Stop learning new topics; redrill weak patterns from your debrief log, run full timed mocks, fix sleep, and rehearse your story bank aloud. The taper converts knowledge into performance — cramming new material now only adds noise.

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Mock incident round'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

quiz.q: The taper period’s rule is:
choices: No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest
quiz.explain: Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

quiz.q: Rubric scoring beats gut feeling because:
choices: It makes weaknesses comparable across mocks — triage needs data
quiz.explain: You can’t triage what you haven’t measured.

quiz.q: An SRE behavioral answer should emphasize:
choices: Decisions under pressure, communication, and systemic learning
quiz.explain: Reliability is a team sport; the graded behaviors are judgment and coordination.

quiz.q: Rehearsing each round’s ‘shape’ helps because:
choices: Interviews grade method under pressure — the shape is the method, made automatic
quiz.explain: Automatic structure frees mental budget for the novel parts of the problem.

cards.front: What’s the case for trunk-based development?
cards.back: Small, frequent merges to main behind feature flags: integration pain drops with merge frequency, main stays releasable, and long-lived branch divergence dies. The interview line: ‘branches are inventory — trunk-based keeps inventory near zero.’

cards.front: What belongs in CI stages, and in what order?
cards.back: Fast-first: lint and unit tests (minutes), then build, integration tests, security scans, artifact publish. The interview line: ‘fail fast and cheap — a 40-minute pipeline that fails at minute 39 teaches nothing quickly.’

cards.front: Why do artifacts and registries matter?
cards.back: Build once, promote the same immutable artifact through environments — registries (container/image, package) make ‘what’s running where’ answerable. The interview line: ‘if you rebuild per environment, you didn’t test what you shipped.’

cards.front: Blue-green vs canary vs rolling?
cards.back: Blue-green: two full environments, instant cutover and rollback — costs double capacity. Canary: new version to a small % first, promote on metrics — safest for risky changes. Rolling: gradual replacement — simplest, slowest rollback. Choose by blast-radius tolerance.

cards.front: What does pipeline-as-code buy you?
cards.back: The pipeline is versioned, reviewed, and reproducible like the app: workflow files in the repo, changes via PR, history in git. The interview line: ‘if the pipeline isn’t in version control, it’s folklore.’

quiz.q: The rollback-vs-fix-forward decision hinges on:
choices: Blast radius and diagnosis confidence — big blast or uncertain cause means roll back
quiz.explain: Uncertain cause + user impact = roll back first, understand second.

quiz.q: Storing CI configuration in the repo enables:
choices: Review, versioning, and reproducibility of the pipeline itself
quiz.explain: Pipeline changes get the same rigor as code changes: PRs, history, rollback.

quiz.q: Canary deployment’s defining feature is:
choices: Releasing to a small subset first and promoting based on observed metrics
quiz.explain: Progressive exposure with metric gates: problems hit 1% before 100%.

quiz.q: Promoting the same immutable artifact through environments ensures:
choices: What you tested is what you ship — no rebuild skew between staging and prod
quiz.explain: Rebuilding per environment invalidates testing; immutable artifacts preserve it.

cards.front: Declarative vs imperative infrastructure?
cards.back: Declarative: state the desired end state, the tool converges (Terraform, K8s manifests) — idempotent and auditable. Imperative: script the steps — flexible but order-dependent and drift-prone. The interview line: ‘I declare the destination; the tool figures out the route.’

cards.front: How do you explain Terraform’s workflow?
cards.back: Write declarative HCL, plan to preview the diff, apply to converge. State tracks reality (remote backend, locking!); modules compose reusable units. The interview traps: state drift, and why plan-before-apply is non-negotiable.

cards.front: How do you discuss state management tradeoffs?
cards.back: Lift state to the lowest common parent first; context for truly global low-churn data (theme, auth) — not as a state manager, since context re-renders all consumers; external stores (Zustand/Redux) for complex shared state with selective subscriptions.

cards.front: How do you structure Terraform modules and composition?
cards.back: Small composable modules (one concern each: network, compute, data), composed in environment roots with explicit inputs — no deep nesting. The interview line: ‘modules are functions; roots are the programs that call them.’

cards.front: What is infrastructure drift, and how do you fight it?
cards.back: Reality diverging from declared config (manual console clicks). Detection: scheduled plan runs that alert on diffs; prevention: make the console read-only, everything through code. The interview line: ‘drift is how outages hide.’

quiz.q: Enforcing policy at plan time (vs after deploy) is better because:
choices: Violations are blocked before they exist — prevention beats detection
quiz.explain: Shift-left for governance: the bad change never reaches the cloud.

quiz.q: The primary defense against drift is:
choices: Everything through code + scheduled plan/detect cycles
quiz.explain: If all changes flow through IaC, reality can’t silently diverge.

quiz.q: Deep module nesting is an anti-pattern because:
choices: Inputs tunnel through layers opaquely — debugging and reuse both suffer
quiz.explain: Flat composition keeps the dependency graph legible; nesting hides it.

quiz.q: React context is a poor state manager for high-churn state because:
choices: Every consumer re-renders on any context value change
quiz.explain: Context has no selectors: one value change re-renders all consumers regardless of what they use.

cards.front: How do Docker layers affect your Dockerfile?
cards.back: Each instruction is a cached layer: order matters — put slow-changing steps (dependency install) before fast-changing ones (code copy) to maximize cache hits. Multi-stage builds keep runtime images small: build in one stage, ship only artifacts.

cards.front: What’s tagging discipline for container registries?
cards.back: Immutable tags per build (git SHA), floating tags (latest) only for convenience — never deploy ‘latest’ to prod. The interview line: ‘mutable tags make ‘what’s running?’ unanswerable.’

cards.front: The Kubernetes objects you must know cold?
cards.back: Pod (smallest unit), Deployment (declarative replicas + rolling updates), Service (stable networking), Ingress (external HTTP routing), ConfigMap/Secret (config separation), PersistentVolume for state. The interview walk: ‘my app runs as a Deployment behind a Service, exposed via Ingress.’

cards.front: How do Deployments, Services, and Ingress fit together?
cards.back: Deployment: declares the desired pods and rolling-update strategy. Service: stable internal endpoint selecting those pods. Ingress: external HTTP routing (host/path → service). The interview line: ‘three layers: run it, find it, expose it.’

cards.front: How do you handle config vs secrets in Kubernetes?
cards.back: ConfigMaps for non-sensitive config, Secrets for sensitive (base64-encoded, not encrypted by default — use external secret managers or encryption at rest for real protection). Mount as env or files; never bake into images. The interview line: ‘config travels with the deployment, not the image.’

quiz.q: Helm’s ‘values’ mechanism lets you:
choices: Deploy the same chart across environments with different configuration
quiz.explain: One chart, many values files: dev/staging/prod differ by values, not by forked manifests.

quiz.q: Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded, which means:
choices: They’re obfuscated, not encrypted — anyone with API access can decode them
quiz.explain: Base64 is encoding, not encryption: etcd encryption or external secret managers provide real protection.

quiz.q: An Ingress resource needs an Ingress controller because:
choices: Ingress is just config — the controller is the actual proxy implementing the routing
quiz.explain: The resource declares intent; the controller (nginx, traefik) does the work.

quiz.q: A Kubernetes Service provides:
choices: Stable networking (DNS + load balancing) for a set of pods
quiz.explain: Pods are ephemeral; the Service gives them a stable virtual IP and DNS name.

cards.front: How do you read logs under pressure?
cards.back: Filter ruthlessly: time window around the incident, the failing service first, errors before info, one clear signal at a time. Correlate with deploys and metric spikes. The interview line: ‘I narrow before I read — logs are guilty until filtered innocent.’

cards.front: How do you actually run five whys on a system?
cards.back: Start from the symptom and ask ‘why’ iteratively, following evidence (logs, metrics, deploys) not hunches — until you reach a process/systemic cause with an action item. The discipline: every ‘why’ needs data, and the fifth why usually points at a missing guardrail.

cards.front: How do you debug network issues methodically?
cards.back: Layer by layer: DNS resolves? (dig/nslookup) TCP connects? (curl -v, telnet) TLS handshakes? (openssl s_client) HTTP responds? Each layer’s test isolates the fault — the interview line: ‘I bisect the stack instead of guessing.’

cards.front: What Kubernetes failure modes must you know?
cards.back: CrashLoopBackOff (bad image/config, failing probes), ImagePullBackOff (registry/auth), OOMKilled (limits vs reality), Pending (no schedulable node/resources), probe misconfiguration (killing healthy pods). The interview line: ‘kubectl describe tells you the story; events are the narrator.’

cards.front: Why do interviewers grade ‘thinking aloud’ in troubleshooting rounds?
cards.back: Because silent debugging is unscoreable: narrating hypotheses, what each command tests, and what the output means lets them evaluate your method. The structure: hypothesis → test → observe → update, said out loud.

quiz.q: Narrating while troubleshooting helps the interviewer assess:
choices: Your diagnostic method — hypotheses, tests, and how you update on evidence
quiz.explain: Method is what’s graded; narration makes the invisible visible.

quiz.q: CrashLoopBackOff most often means:
choices: The container starts then exits — bad command, missing config, or failing startup probe
quiz.explain: The kubelet keeps retrying a container that can’t stay alive; describe/events reveal why it dies.

quiz.q: curl -v failing at ‘Could not resolve host’ means:
choices: DNS failure — the name never became an IP
quiz.explain: Resolution happens before any connection: the fault is in DNS, not the server.

quiz.q: Five whys stops being useful when:
choices: Answers become speculation without evidence — each why needs data
quiz.explain: Whys without evidence are storytelling; the method works when each level is grounded in telemetry.

cards.front: What does a good platform-build scaffold include?
cards.back: Repo layout (app + infra + pipeline), VPC via Terraform, cluster bootstrap scripted, CI pipeline, GitOps deploy — each piece documented as a deliverable. The interview line: ‘the scaffold is the platform’s first impression.’

cards.front: How do you discuss undefined behavior in a C interview?
cards.back: As the compiler’s license to assume: signed overflow, null dereference, use-after-free, data races — ‘anything can happen’ includes ‘works until the optimizer upgrades.’ The interview line: ‘I write so UB can’t happen; sanitizers prove it.’

cards.front: What is GitOps, concretely?
cards.back: Git as the single source of truth for desired state; an agent (Argo CD/Flux) continuously reconciles the cluster to it. Pull-based, auditable, self-healing: drift gets reverted automatically, and every change is a git commit.

cards.front: Why is documentation a deliverable in platform work?
cards.back: Because platforms have customers: runbooks, ADRs, and onboarding docs are the API of the platform team. The interview line: ‘undocumented automation is a ticket queue with extra steps.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Repo scaffold: app plus Dockerfile'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

quiz.q: An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) captures:
choices: The decision, its context, alternatives considered, and consequences — why, not just what
quiz.explain: Future-you needs the reasoning, not just the outcome; ADRs preserve the why.

quiz.q: In GitOps, cluster drift is handled by:
choices: The agent reconciling actual state back to the git-declared desired state
quiz.explain: Continuous reconciliation closes the loop: declared state wins automatically.

quiz.q: Signed integer overflow in C is:
choices: Undefined behavior — the optimizer may assume it never happens
quiz.explain: Compilers exploit the UB assumption for optimization; ‘works in debug’ proves nothing.

quiz.q: Scripting the cluster bootstrap (vs clicking) matters because:
choices: It’s reproducible and reviewable — the cluster becomes code, not folklore
quiz.explain: Unscripted setup can’t be rebuilt, reviewed, or audited.

cards.front: How do behavioral rounds differ for SREs?
cards.back: They probe ownership under pressure: on-call stories, incident decisions, disagreements about risk, and learning from outages — all STAR, all blameless. The interview line: ‘SRE behavioral rounds grade how I act when the pager fires.’

cards.front: What’s the STAR structure, and why does it work for behavioral rounds?
cards.back: Situation (2 sentences of context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what YOU did — the bulk), Result (measurable outcome + lesson). It works because interviewers score evidence of behavior, and STAR forces a complete evidence unit.

cards.front: What questions should you ask the interviewer?

cards.front: How do you handle offer and negotiation basics?
cards.back: Know your market range from data (levels.fyi, peers), let them anchor first when possible, negotiate the whole package (base, equity, bonus, start date) — never just base salary — and get everything in writing. The interview line: ‘I negotiate once, informed and in good faith.’

quiz.q: Negotiating only base salary is weak because:

quiz.explain: The package is the number; single-dimension negotiation leaves money unclaimed.

quiz.q: The strongest interviewer question reveals:

quiz.explain: You’re interviewing them too: these answers predict your actual day-to-day.

quiz.q: In a STAR answer, the ‘A’ should emphasize:
quiz.explain: ‘We’ stories hide your contribution — interviewers evaluate you, so make your decisions explicit.

quiz.q: An SRE behavioral answer should emphasize:
choices: Decisions under pressure, communication, and systemic learning
quiz.explain: Reliability is a team sport; the graded behaviors are judgment and coordination.

cards.front: Regions vs Availability Zones?
cards.back: Region: geographic area. AZ: isolated data center(s) within a region with independent power/network. Design rule: run across ≥2 AZs for HA; regions are for disaster recovery and data residency. The interview line: ‘one AZ is a single point of failure.’

cards.front: What is the shared-responsibility model?
cards.back: The provider secures OF the cloud (physical, hypervisor, network fabric); you secure what’s IN it (data, IAM, OS, app config). The interview trap: ‘the cloud is secure’ — no, your S3 bucket policy is your job.

cards.front: What does Docker actually give you?
cards.back: A portable, reproducible runtime: the image bundles code + dependencies + OS userland, so ‘works on my machine’ dies. Containers share the host kernel (lighter than VMs, weaker isolation) — and the interview follow-up is always about image size and layer caching.

cards.front: CapEx vs OpEx in cloud interviews?
cards.back: CapEx: buy servers upfront (fixed, depreciating). OpEx: pay per use (variable, scales with demand). Cloud’s pitch is OpEx agility — but the honest follow-up is FinOps: without governance, variable spend surprises you.

cards.front: Vendor-neutral vs vendor-specific knowledge?
cards.back: Neutral: concepts that transfer (VPCs, IAM, queues, object storage). Specific: the console clicks and service quirks. The interview line: ‘I learn the concept once, the console twice — concepts transfer, click-paths don’t.’

quiz.q: Leading with vendor-neutral concepts in an interview is strong because:
choices: It proves transferable understanding, not memorized console paths
quiz.explain: Concepts survive provider changes; click-path knowledge expires with the UI.

quiz.q: Cloud’s OpEx model primarily buys:
choices: Agility — spend scales with demand instead of upfront provisioning
quiz.explain: Pay-per-use trades fixed capacity bets for variable spend — with cost governance as the required discipline.

quiz.q: Containers differ from VMs in that they:
choices: Share the host OS kernel instead of virtualizing hardware
quiz.explain: No guest kernel per container: faster startup, denser packing, but a shared kernel attack surface.

quiz.q: Under shared responsibility, an open S3 bucket is:
choices: The customer’s fault — data access control is in the customer’s layer
quiz.explain: The provider secures the service; you configure who can read your objects.

cards.front: VPC, subnets, route tables — the 60-second version?
cards.back: VPC: your isolated network. Subnets: public (route to internet gateway) vs private (no direct inbound, NAT for outbound). Route tables decide where packets go; security groups (stateful, instance-level) and NACLs (stateless, subnet-level) filter them.

cards.front: LCP, INP, CLS — what does each measure?
cards.back: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint): loading — when the main content appears. INP (Interaction to Next Paint): responsiveness — worst-case input latency. CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift): visual stability — unexpected movement. For all three, lower is better.

cards.front: What do cloud load balancers do beyond spreading traffic?
cards.back: Health checks (route only to healthy targets), TLS termination, sticky sessions when needed, and L7 routing (path/host rules). The interview line: ‘the LB is the first reliability device in the path.’

cards.front: How do you discuss DNS in cloud interviews?
cards.back: Public DNS for the world, private hosted zones for internal service discovery, TTLs controlling change propagation, and health-checked routing policies for failover. The interview line: ‘DNS is the control plane everyone forgets until it breaks.’

cards.front: NAT vs VPN vs peering?
cards.back: NAT: private resources reach the internet outbound. VPN: encrypted tunnel extending your network (site-to-site or client). Peering: private VPC-to-VPC connectivity without internet. The interview line: ‘each answers a different ‘how do these networks talk’ question.’

quiz.q: VPC flow logs show:
choices: Allowed/rejected IP traffic metadata — who tried to reach whom
quiz.explain: Flow logs are the packet-level audit trail for security-group and routing diagnosis.

quiz.q: VPC peering is preferred over public IPs for inter-VPC traffic because:
choices: Traffic stays on the private backbone — no internet exposure
quiz.explain: Private routing beats public routing for both security and latency.

quiz.q: A low TTL on a DNS record is used when:
choices: You expect to change the target soon and need fast propagation
quiz.explain: Low TTL trades query volume for agility: changes propagate as fast as the TTL allows.

quiz.q: Load balancer health checks matter because:
choices: Traffic must avoid dead targets — the LB routes only to passing instances
quiz.explain: Without health checks, the balancer sprays traffic onto broken instances.

cards.front: How do you handle file uploads at scale?
cards.back: Direct-to-object-storage uploads (presigned URLs — the app server never proxies bytes), async processing (thumbnails, virus scan) via queues, CDN in front for reads. The interview line: ‘bytes never touch my app servers.’

cards.front: What do managed SQL services buy you?
cards.back: Backups, patching, failover, and read replicas handled by the provider — you keep schema design and query tuning. The interview line: ‘I outsource the undifferentiated heavy lifting, not the data model.’

cards.front: How do you discuss managed NoSQL in a cloud interview?
cards.back: By access pattern: key-value (DynamoDB-style single-digit-ms lookups), document (flexible JSON), wide-column (massive write scale). The interview line: ‘I choose the NoSQL by the query pattern, then take the managed version of that choice.’

cards.front: How do you discuss caching in a cloud interview?
cards.back: What to cache (read-heavy, slow-changing), where (CDN edge, app cache, DB query cache), invalidation strategy, and the failure story (thundering herd, stale reads). The interview line: ‘caching is a tradeoff with an invalidation plan, not a speedup.’

cards.front: How do you manage data lifecycle and tiering?
cards.back: Classify by access pattern and compliance needs: hot (frequent, fast storage), warm, cold/archive (cheap, slow retrieval). Automate transitions with lifecycle policies; the interview line: ‘every byte has a cost curve — tiering matches cost to value.’

quiz.q: RPO and RTO define:
choices: How much data loss is tolerable and how fast recovery must complete
quiz.explain: RPO bounds data loss (backup frequency); RTO bounds downtime (recovery speed).

quiz.q: Archiving compliance data to glacier-class storage is justified because:
choices: Rarely-accessed retention data shouldn’t pay hot-storage prices
quiz.explain: Storage cost should follow access frequency; compliance retention is the classic cold tier.

quiz.q: Every caching decision must name:
choices: The invalidation strategy — stale data is caching’s permanent tax
quiz.explain: Cache without an invalidation story is a future incident.

quiz.q: Managed NoSQL’s pitch is:
choices: Operational burden offloaded — scaling, patching, and failover handled
quiz.explain: You keep the data-model decisions; the provider keeps the cluster healthy.

cards.front: What are the incident command roles?
cards.back: Incident Commander (decides, coordinates — doesn’t debug), Communications (status updates, stakeholders), Scribe (timeline), plus subject-matter experts debugging. The IC’s job is the incident, not the keyboard.

cards.front: How do you do IAM least privilege in practice?
cards.back: Roles over users, policies scoped to specific actions on specific resources, no wildcards in production, permission boundaries and SCPs as guardrails, regular access reviews. The interview line: ‘every permission has a reason and an expiry conversation.’

cards.front: What makes an API ‘RESTful’ in an interview answer?
cards.back: Resources as nouns in URLs, HTTP verbs as actions, status codes as the contract (200/201/400/401/403/404/429/500), stateless requests, and versioning — then the judgment calls: pagination, filtering, and idempotency.

cards.front: How do you manage secrets in the cloud?
cards.back: Dedicated secret managers (rotation, audit, fine-grained access) — never env files in repos, never baked into images. Apps fetch at runtime with their workload role. The interview line: ‘secrets are fetched, not shipped.’

cards.front: What are cloud guardrails?
cards.back: Preventive: SCPs and permission boundaries that make bad actions impossible. Detective: Config rules and CloudTrail audit trails that catch what happened. The interview line: ‘guardrails make the safe path the easy path.’

quiz.q: CloudTrail’s primary purpose is:
choices: An audit log of who did what via the API — the forensic record
quiz.explain: Every API call recorded with identity and time: the basis for incident forensics and compliance.

quiz.q: Baking secrets into container images is wrong because:
choices: Anyone with registry access gets the secrets — images are widely shared artifacts
quiz.explain: Images travel through registries and caches; secrets must be injected at runtime, not build time.

quiz.q: Creating the same resource twice with POST vs PUT: the key difference is:
choices: PUT is idempotent — repeating it has the same effect; POST is not guaranteed to be
quiz.explain: Idempotency is the contract: safe retries depend on it.

quiz.q: An IAM policy with Action: ‘*’ on Resource: ‘*’ is:
choices: A violation of least privilege — blast radius is the whole account
quiz.explain: Wildcard-everything grants total control; compromise of those credentials compromises the account.

cards.back: Constraints as linear equations the solver satisfies; intrinsic content size vs explicit constraints; ambiguity and conflicts (and how you read the logs); performance (flatten deep hierarchies). The interview line: ‘I think in constraints, not frames.’

cards.front: Walk the classic three-tier cloud architecture.
cards.back: Presentation (ALB + CDN) → application (auto-scaled compute across AZs) → data (managed DB with replicas, caches). Public subnets for the LB, private for app and data. The interview line: ‘tiers are failure and scaling boundaries, not just boxes.’

cards.front: How do you present a cloud architecture with cost honesty?
cards.back: IaC for the whole stack (reproducible, reviewable), a cost estimate with assumptions stated (requests, storage, transfer — transfer is the surprise line item), and the tradeoff: ‘here’s what drives the bill and the lever that moves it.’

cards.front: What’s an ADR, and why do architects write them?
cards.back: Architecture Decision Record: the decision, context, alternatives considered, and consequences — the ‘why’ behind the design. Paired with a failure-mode review (what breaks, how we degrade). The interview line: ‘ADRs are how architecture survives team turnover.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Requirements and constraints'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

quiz.q: A failure-mode review asks:
choices: What breaks, how the system degrades, and whether that degradation is acceptable
quiz.explain: Designing for the unhappy path is what separates architecture from diagramming.

quiz.q: Data transfer is the classic cloud cost surprise because:
choices: Architectures that chat across AZs/regions pay per GB — it compounds silently
quiz.explain: Egress and cross-AZ transfer bill by volume; chatty designs pay continuously.

quiz.q: The app tier sits in private subnets because:
choices: Only the load balancer needs internet exposure — app servers stay unreachable directly
quiz.explain: Minimizing internet-facing surface: one controlled entry point, defense in depth behind it.

quiz.q: An ‘ambiguous layout’ warning means:
choices: The constraints don’t fully determine position/size — the solver is guessing
quiz.explain: Ambiguity = under-constrained; conflicts = over-constrained. Different problems, different fixes.

cards.front: How do you discuss the OWASP Top 10 without just listing it?
cards.back: As risk categories with a current example each: injection, broken access control, crypto failures, SSRF, and so on — then pivot to YOUR experience: ‘here’s how I found one in code review and what the fix was.’ Categories frame; stories score.

cards.front: XSS types and the fix?
cards.back: Stored (persisted, served to victims), reflected (in a crafted URL), DOM-based (client-side sink). The fix: output encoding/contextual escaping, Content-Security-Policy as defense in depth, and frameworks’ auto-escaping — never innerHTML with untrusted data.

cards.front: What auth flaws do you hunt in code review?
cards.back: Broken authentication (credential stuffing without rate limits, weak session handling), broken object-level authorization (IDOR), missing function-level checks, JWT ‘none’ algorithm or missing expiry validation. The interview line: ‘I check every endpoint for ‘who can call this’ — not just the login page.’

cards.front: What’s SSRF and why is it nasty in the cloud?
cards.back: Server-Side Request Forgery: the server fetches attacker-chosen URLs — in cloud, that means the instance metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) and credential theft. Fixes: allowlist egress, validate/sanitize URLs, block metadata IP, IMDSv2. (Deserialization: never unserialize untrusted data — it’s remote code execution.)

cards.front: What do you look for in a security code review?
cards.back: Injection sinks, auth checks on every route, crypto done right (no custom algorithms), secrets handling, error messages that don’t leak internals, and dependency versions. The interview line: ‘I review the trust boundaries first — where untrusted data enters.’

quiz.q: Error messages that include stack traces are a finding because:
choices: They leak internals (paths, versions, queries) that aid attackers
quiz.explain: Information disclosure sharpens every subsequent attack; production errors stay generic.

quiz.q: SSRF’s cloud nightmare scenario is:
choices: Hitting the instance metadata service to steal temporary credentials
quiz.explain: The metadata endpoint is one hop from the vulnerable server — credentials included.

quiz.q: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) means:
choices: Changing an object ID in a request accesses another user’s data — missing authorization check
quiz.explain: Authentication proves who you are; authorization must then prove you may touch this object.

quiz.q: The root fix for XSS is:
choices: Context-appropriate output encoding of untrusted data (+ CSP in depth)
quiz.explain: XSS is code/data confusion in the browser; encoding keeps untrusted data as data.

cards.front: Walk the TLS handshake at interview depth.
cards.back: ClientHello (ciphers) → ServerHello + certificate → key exchange (ECDHE for forward secrecy) → encrypted session. Validate: cert chain to a trusted root, hostname match, expiry — and pinning for high-value mobile/API clients.

cards.front: How do you talk about firewalls and segmentation?
cards.back: Defense in depth through zones: public DMZ, app tier, data tier — traffic only flows where explicitly allowed, east-west as well as north-south. The interview line: ‘segmentation turns one breach into a contained incident instead of a network-wide event.’

cards.front: What does zero trust actually require?
cards.back: ‘Never trust, always verify’: identity-based access (not network location), least privilege, device posture, continuous verification, micro-segmentation. The interview line: ‘the VPN perimeter is dead; every request authenticates and authorizes.’

cards.front: What’s DNS security in practice?
cards.back: DNSSEC for integrity (responses are signed), DoH/DoT for query privacy, monitoring for tunneling/exfiltration (long odd queries), and registrar hygiene (locks, MFA). The interview line: ‘DNS is trusted by everything and verified by almost nothing — I verify.’

cards.front: How do you discuss DDoS mitigation?
cards.back: Layers: edge absorption (CDN/anycast scrubbing), rate limiting, WAF rules for L7, and capacity headroom. Distinguish volumetric (bandwidth) from application-layer (expensive requests) — they need different defenses. The interview line: ‘you don’t outrun a botnet; you absorb and filter at the edge.’

quiz.q: Wireshark showing repeated TCP retransmissions indicates:
choices: Packet loss or an unresponsive peer — a network-path problem, not application logic
quiz.explain: Retransmits are the transport layer saying ‘my packets aren’t getting through.’

quiz.q: Application-layer (L7) DDoS differs from volumetric in that it:
choices: Uses expensive legitimate-looking requests — filtering needs behavioral/WAF rules, not just bandwidth
quiz.explain: A few thousand costly requests can hurt more than gigabits of junk; defense is semantic.

quiz.q: DNS tunneling exfiltrates data by:
choices: Encoding data in DNS queries to an attacker-controlled domain — DNS is rarely filtered
quiz.explain: DNS’s ubiquity makes it a covert channel; monitoring query patterns catches it.

quiz.q: Zero trust’s core shift is:
choices: Access decisions from identity and context, not network location
quiz.explain: Being inside the network grants nothing; every request proves who/what it is.

cards.front: Symmetric vs asymmetric crypto — the interview version?
cards.back: Symmetric (AES): one shared key, fast — for bulk data. Asymmetric (RSA/ECDH): key pairs, slow — for key exchange and signatures. Hybrid in practice: asymmetric establishes, symmetric encrypts. The interview line: ‘asymmetric for trust, symmetric for speed.’

cards.front: How do you store passwords — the security interview version?
cards.back: Argon2id (or bcrypt) with unique per-user salts and a tuned work factor; pepper via KMS/HSM as defense in depth. Never MD5/SHA-256 alone (too fast — GPUs crack them), never reversible encryption.

cards.front: What’s ‘TLS in practice’ beyond the handshake?
cards.back: Version and cipher hygiene (TLS 1.2+, strong suites), cert lifecycle (automation via ACME, expiry monitoring), HSTS, and pinning for high-value clients. The interview line: ‘handshake knowledge gets you hired; lifecycle hygiene keeps you employed.’

cards.front: What does real key management look like?
cards.back: Keys in a KMS/HSM, never in code or repos; envelope encryption; rotation on a schedule and on incident; separate keys per environment/data class; audit every use. The interview line: ‘if I can see the key in the repo, we’ve already lost.’

cards.front: What does ‘randomness done right’ mean?
cards.back: Cryptographic randomness (CSPRNG: /dev/urandom, secrets module) for keys, tokens, and nonces — never Math.random() or seeded PRNGs for security purposes. The interview line: ‘predictable randomness is no randomness.’

quiz.q: Custom crypto is dangerous because:
choices: Subtle flaws survive testing and review — even experts get it wrong; use vetted primitives
quiz.explain: Cryptographic failures are silent until exploited; peer-reviewed primitives are the only sane choice.

quiz.q: Math.random() is unfit for security tokens because:
choices: It’s a predictable PRNG — outputs can be reconstructed by attackers
quiz.explain: Non-cryptographic PRNGs have observable state; CSPRNGs are designed to resist prediction.

quiz.q: Key rotation limits damage because:
choices: A leaked key has a bounded useful lifetime
quiz.explain: Rotation shrinks the window where a compromised key is valuable.

quiz.q: Certificate expiry monitoring matters because:
choices: Expired certs are a top-5 outage cause — entirely preventable with automation
quiz.explain: Letting certs expire is an unforced outage; ACME + monitoring ends it.

cards.front: How do you use MITRE ATT&CK in an interview?
cards.back: As a shared map of adversary behavior: tactics (why — initial access, persistence, exfiltration) → techniques (how). Detection engineering maps log sources to techniques and writes detections per technique — coverage measured against the matrix, not vibes.

cards.front: What makes detection engineering real?
cards.back: Detections mapped to ATT&CK techniques, built on log sources you’ve verified produce the needed telemetry, tuned for signal (precision/recall on alerts), and tested with simulated adversary activity. The interview line: ‘a detection without a tested log source is a hope.’

cards.front: Walk the incident response phases.
cards.back: Preparation → Detection & Analysis → Containment → Eradication → Recovery → Lessons Learned (NIST 800-61). The interview emphasis: contain before you eradicate (don’t tip off the adversary / destroy evidence), and lessons-learned feeds back into preparation.

cards.front: How do you tell a breach story in an interview?
cards.back: Blameless framing, the timeline as you understood it then, what the investigation actually showed, the action items with owners — and what you personally changed afterward. The interview line: ‘I talk about what the incident taught the system, not who failed.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'ATT&CK as a map'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

quiz.q: A breach story should emphasize:
choices: Timeline, evidence-driven findings, and systemic fixes with owners
quiz.explain: Interviewers score learning and systems thinking — blame and heroics score nothing.

quiz.q: Containment comes before eradication because:
choices: You stop the bleeding and preserve evidence before removing the threat
quiz.explain: Eradicating first can destroy forensic evidence and alert the adversary mid-investigation.

quiz.q: A detection rule needs tuning because:
choices: Untuned rules alert on benign activity — alert fatigue kills the SOC’s trust
quiz.explain: Precision matters as much as recall: a noisy rule gets ignored, then the real alert dies in the noise.

quiz.q: ATT&CK’s tactics vs techniques distinction is:
choices: Tactics are adversary goals; techniques are how they achieve them
quiz.explain: The hierarchy lets defenders map ‘what could happen’ to ‘what we’d see’ systematically.

cards.front: When do you reach for two pointers?
cards.back: Ordered data and pair-finding: opposite ends for sorted two-sum or container-with-most-water; same-direction fast/slow pointers for cycle detection or in-place dedup — O(n) time, O(1) space. Name which variant and why.

cards.front: How do you speed-rep DSA fundamentals?
cards.back: Pattern batches under time: trees/graphs/heaps one session (traversals, BFS/DFS, top-k), DP basics the next (1D ladder, knapsack shapes) — always stating complexity aloud. The interview line: ‘speed reps build the reflex; the debrief builds the skill.’

cards.front: How do you handle the 30-minute coding bar?
cards.back: Budget aloud: 5 min clarify + plan, 20 min code, 5 min test. Start with brute force stated and its complexity (it buys time and shows honesty), then optimize the bottleneck. A working brute force beats a half-written optimal.

cards.front: Why say complexity out loud?
cards.back: Because the interviewer can’t grade silent thought: stating ‘this is O(n) time, O(1) space because…’ at each step turns reasoning into evidence. It’s also your early-warning system — saying it forces you to check it.

cards.front: How do you review wrong answers productively?
cards.back: Classify the miss: wrong pattern, bug in implementation, complexity fumble, or time management — then redrill the class, not just the problem. The interview line: ‘I fix the category, not the instance.’

quiz.q: Redrilling the miss category (not just the problem) works because:
choices: Interviews test categories under new disguises — the instance never repeats
quiz.explain: The next problem will wear a different costume; the category is what transfers.

quiz.q: Stating complexity aloud during coding:
choices: Makes your reasoning gradable and forces self-checks
quiz.explain: Verbalized reasoning is scorable reasoning — and it catches your own mistakes mid-stream.

quiz.q: Stating the brute force first is strong because:
choices: It shows honest complexity reasoning and gives a working fallback while you optimize
quiz.explain: A correct slow solution on the board beats a blank editor; optimization then has a baseline.

quiz.q: Speed reps should always include stating complexity aloud because:
choices: The interview grades the analysis as well as the code — rehearse both together
quiz.explain: Rehearsing code without narration trains half the interview.

cards.front: How do you open a system design round?
cards.back: Requirements before architecture: restate functional requirements (what the system does), then non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency). Scoping first proves you design the right system — candidates who draw boxes before asking get failed.

cards.front: How do you do API + data-model design in a system-design rep?
cards.back: Resources and verbs first, then the storage that serves the access patterns — the two designed together, since API shape constrains queries and data shape constrains the API. The interview line: ‘the API and the model are one decision, not two.’

cards.front: How do you talk about scaling levers?
cards.back: The three moves: shard the data (split the load), cache the hot paths (skip the work), queue the spikes (defer the work). The interview line: ‘scaling is choosing which of the three each bottleneck needs.’

cards.front: How do you prep the classic designs (shortener, feed, chat)?
cards.back: One page each: requirements, estimation, the 2–3 key decisions, the scaling story. The classics are classics because they each teach one lesson — shortener: IDs and caching; feed: fan-out; chat: real-time. The interview line: ‘I learn the lesson, not the diagram.’

cards.front: How do you do bottleneck analysis in a design round?
cards.back: Follow the request path and ask ‘what breaks first as load grows 10x?’ at each hop — then apply the right lever (shard/cache/queue) to that hop. The interview line: ‘bottlenecks are found by walking the path, not by guessing.’

quiz.q: Labeling arrows with what flows matters because:
choices: Unlabeled arrows hide the data story — the labels are where the design lives
quiz.explain: Architecture is data in motion; unlabeled arrows are just boxes.

quiz.q: Asking ‘what breaks first at 10x’ is the right question because:
choices: It forces ordered thinking about limits instead of vague ‘it scales’ claims
quiz.explain: Scaling claims need a named first failure; otherwise they’re wishes.

quiz.q: Learning the lesson (not the diagram) matters because:
choices: Interviewers vary the problem — the transferable insight is what repeats
quiz.explain: The next question won’t be the shortener; the ID-generation insight will recur.

quiz.q: Queues handle spikes while caches handle hot data because:
choices: Queues defer work in time; caches skip work entirely — different bottlenecks, different tools
quiz.explain: Time-shifting vs work-avoidance: match the lever to the bottleneck’s nature.

cards.front: What’s the STAR structure, and why does it work for behavioral rounds?
cards.back: Situation (2 sentences of context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what YOU did — the bulk), Result (measurable outcome + lesson). It works because interviewers score evidence of behavior, and STAR forces a complete evidence unit.

cards.front: How do you cover conflict, failure, and leadership stories?

cards.front: How do you answer ‘Why this company?’ convincingly?

cards.front: What questions should you ask the interviewer?

cards.front: Why practice behavioral answers aloud — and record them?

cards.back: Four timed rounds back-to-back (coding, design, domain deep-dive, behavioral) with a partner playing interviewer, scored against a rubric, then a weakness-targeting week on the lowest scores. The point: stamina and context-switching are skills you train.

cards.front: What are the incident command roles?
cards.back: Incident Commander (decides, coordinates — doesn’t debug), Communications (status updates, stakeholders), Scribe (timeline), plus subject-matter experts debugging. The IC’s job is the incident, not the keyboard.

cards.front: How do you score yourself against an interview rubric?
cards.back: Fixed axes per round type: correctness, complexity analysis, communication, time management, tradeoffs named. Score honestly after every mock; the rubric turns feelings into data. The interview line: ‘I grade myself the way they’ll grade me.’

cards.front: What’s a weakness-targeting week?
cards.back: One week between full-loop simulation and the real loop, spent only on the lowest rubric scores: targeted drills, one more mock per weak area, then rest. The interview line: ‘the week has one job — raise the floor.’

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?
cards.back: Stop learning new topics; redrill weak patterns from your debrief log, run full timed mocks, fix sleep, and rehearse your story bank aloud. The taper converts knowledge into performance — cramming new material now only adds noise.

quiz.q: The taper period’s rule is:
choices: No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest
quiz.explain: Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

quiz.q: Targeting the floor (not the ceiling) is right because:
choices: Offers are lost on weak rounds, not won on strong ones — the minimum decides
quiz.explain: Interview loops grade the weakest link; raising it raises the whole loop.

quiz.q: Rubric scoring beats gut feeling because:
choices: It makes weaknesses comparable across mocks — triage needs data
quiz.explain: You can’t triage what you haven’t measured.

scriptLabs.title: Error-budget calculator
scriptLabs.brief: Turn SLO math into code: given total requests, failed requests, and an SLO, compute the percentage of the error budget consumed. The arithmetic behind every burn-rate conversation.
scriptLabs.starter:
def budget_consumed(total_requests, failed_requests, slo):
    """Return the % of the error budget consumed (0-100+, may exceed 100).

    slo: e.g. 0.999 for a 99.9% SLO.
    """
    # TODO: allowed failures = total * (1 - slo); consumed % = failed / allowed * 100.
    pass
scriptLabs.hint: Budget = total × (1 − SLO); consumed % = failed ÷ allowed × 100. Guard the zero-allowed edge case.
scriptLabs.solution:
def budget_consumed(total_requests, failed_requests, slo):
    allowed = total_requests * (1 - slo)
    if allowed <= 0:
        return 100.0 if failed_requests > 0 else 0.0
    return (failed_requests / allowed) * 100

# Example: 1M requests, 500 failed, 99.9% SLO -> 50% of budget consumed.
print(budget_consumed(1_000_000, 500, 0.999))

scriptLabs.title: Production-ready Deployment manifest
scriptLabs.brief: Write a Kubernetes Deployment you’d defend in an interview: replicas, probes, resource requests/limits, and labels. The manifest is the artifact; the narration is the score.
scriptLabs.starter:
# TODO: complete this Deployment for a web API named 'api' (image api:1.4.2).
# Requirements: 3 replicas, readiness + liveness probes on /healthz,
# CPU/memory requests AND limits, app=api labels.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
scriptLabs.hint: Probes need httpGet on /healthz with initialDelaySeconds; resources need both requests and limits; matchLabels must equal the pod template labels.
scriptLabs.solution:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
  labels:
    app: api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: api:1.4.2
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "250m"
            memory: "256Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "1000m"
            memory: "512Mi"

scriptLabs.title: Burn-rate alert rule (Prometheus)
scriptLabs.brief: Write the fast-burn Prometheus alert you’d actually ship: budget-consumption ratio over two windows, a for-duration, and a severity. Symptom-based alerting, as the module teaches.
scriptLabs.starter:
# TODO: alert when the service burns its 99.9% SLO error budget too fast.
# Metrics: http_requests_total, http_requests_failed_total (counter, label-free).
# Requirements: burn-rate expression, 'for' duration, severity label, summary annotation.
groups:
- name: slo-burn
  rules:
scriptLabs.hint: Burn rate = failed-rate / (total-rate × budget-ratio). For 99.9%, the budget ratio is 0.001; alert when the ratio exceeds ~14x over both a 1h and a 5m window.
scriptLabs.solution:
groups:
- name: slo-burn
  rules:
  - alert: HighErrorBudgetBurn
    expr: |
      (
        sum(rate(http_requests_failed_total[1h]))
        /
        sum(rate(http_requests_total[1h]))
      ) > 0.001 * 14.4
      and
      (
        sum(rate(http_requests_failed_total[5m]))
        /
        sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
      ) > 0.001 * 14.4
    for: 15m
    labels:
      severity: critical
    annotations:
      summary: "Error budget burning 14x faster than the 99.9% SLO allows"

scriptLabs.title: Triage runbook: pods CrashLooping
scriptLabs.brief: Write the ordered triage script you’d narrate in a live troubleshooting round: from symptom to cause in kubectl commands. Hypothesis → test → observe, said out loud.
scriptLabs.starter:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Triage: pods for deployment 'api' are CrashLooping.
# TODO: ordered commands — status, events, logs, resources, recent changes.
set -euo pipefail
NS=prod
scriptLabs.hint: Order: what’s happening (get/describe) → why it dies (logs of the previous container) → resource pressure (top) → what changed (rollout history).
scriptLabs.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Triage: 'api' pods CrashLooping in prod.
set -euo pipefail
NS=prod

echo "== 1. What is happening?"
kubectl get pods -n "$NS" -l app=api
kubectl describe deployment api -n "$NS" | tail -20

echo "== 2. Why did the container die? (previous container logs)"
kubectl logs -n "$NS" -l app=api --previous --tail=100 || true

echo "== 3. Resource pressure?"
kubectl top pods -n "$NS" -l app=api || true

echo "== 4. What changed recently?"
kubectl rollout history deployment/api -n "$NS"

echo "== 5. Events tell the story"
kubectl get events -n "$NS" --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20

scenarios.title: Incident command: sev-1 checkout outage
scenarios.context: 02:14. Pager: checkout error rate 40% and climbing. You’re the on-call SRE and incident commander.

steps.prompt: First action in the opening minutes?

options.text: Declare the incident, assume IC, open the bridge and the #incident channel
options.why: Command before debugging: declaring focuses the response, the bridge gathers experts, and the IC coordinates instead of keyboard-diving.

options.text: SSH in and start debugging the checkout service alone
options.why: Solo debugging abandons command — nobody coordinates, comms go silent, and parallel work collides.

options.text: Page the entire engineering org immediately
options.why: Paging everyone is noise; page the service owners and scale only if the blast radius demands it.

options.text: Wait 10 minutes to see if it recovers on its own
options.why: 40% errors and climbing is user harm now; waiting converts an incident into a longer incident.

steps.prompt: Five minutes in, no mitigation yet. What do you communicate?

options.text: Post impact-first updates to #incident every ~15 minutes: who’s affected, what we’re doing, when the next update lands
options.why: Cadenced, impact-first comms prevent the second outage (confusion); ‘no update’ is itself an update.

options.text: Stay silent until there’s a fix to announce
options.why: Silence during an outage breeds rumors and duplicate escalations — comms is part of the response.

options.text: Post raw stack traces and theories as they occur
options.why: Unfiltered debugging noise confuses stakeholders; the comms role translates signal for the audience.

options.text: Email the CEO directly with early speculation
options.why: Escalation without facts creates pressure without progress; comms goes through the incident channel.

steps.prompt: You suspect the 02:00 deploy. Mitigation vs root cause — what now?

options.text: Roll back the deploy first (mitigate), investigate the root cause after traffic recovers
options.why: Mitigate first, understand second: every minute of 40% errors is user harm, and the rollback is the fastest hypothesis test.

options.text: Find the exact root cause before touching anything
options.why: Diagnosis-before-mitigation maximizes outage duration; the incident lifecycle puts mitigation first.

options.text: Scale up the checkout pods — more capacity fixes everything
options.why: Scaling a broken deploy multiplies the brokenness; capacity treats a symptom you haven’t diagnosed.

options.text: Restart all pods simultaneously
options.why: A full restart is a full outage during the restart — and it destroys the evidence you need.

steps.prompt: The incident is resolved. What makes the postmortem useful?

options.text: Blameless timeline, plural root causes, and action items with owners and dates
options.why: Blamelessness gets honest data; owned action items are the postmortem’s actual product — the document is just the vehicle.

options.text: A detailed account of who made the bad deploy
options.why: Blame produces cover stories in future incidents; systems and process are the fixable units.

options.text: A brief ‘all good now’ note to close the ticket
options.why: No learning, no action items — the same incident will recur on schedule.

options.text: Only the timeline, no action items
options.why: A timeline without action items is a history lesson; prevention requires owned follow-through.

scenarios.title: Design round: deployment pipeline
scenarios.context: ‘Design the CI/CD pipeline for our user-facing API.’ The interviewer wants decisions, not a tool list.

steps.prompt: Deployment strategy for the user-facing API?

options.text: Canary: small % first, promote on error-rate/latency gates, automated rollback
options.why: Progressive exposure with metric gates bounds blast radius — the right default for user-facing services.

options.text: Big-bang deploy to all instances at once — fastest
options.why: Fastest to deploy, fastest to outage: 100% of users meet every bad release simultaneously.

options.text: Manual SCP of binaries to each server
options.why: Unauditable, unrepeatable, unrollbackable — the opposite of a pipeline.

options.text: Deploy on Fridays to get it over with
options.why: Timing theater instead of safety engineering; the strategy should make any day safe.

options.text: In CI, blocking merge on critical findings — shift-left
options.why: Vulnerabilities found at commit time are cheapest to fix; blocking the merge makes the gate mechanical.

options.text: After deploy, scanned in production
options.why: Scanning prod finds vulnerabilities you’ve already shipped to attackers.

options.text: Once a year during the audit
options.why: Annual scanning leaves 364 days of unexamined changes — security theater.

options.text: Nowhere — developers are trusted
options.why: Trust isn’t a control; even excellent developers ship vulnerable dependencies unknowingly.

steps.prompt: The interviewer asks: ‘how do you roll back?’

options.text: One command redeploys the previous immutable artifact; DB migrations are backward-compatible (expand-contract)
options.why: Rollback is only real if it’s rehearsed, one command, and the data layer tolerates the old code.

options.text: ‘We’d fix forward — rollbacks are for the weak’
options.why: Fix-forward during an active outage gambles user impact on debugging speed.

options.text: Restore from last night’s backup
options.why: Backup restore loses all data since the backup and takes far longer than an artifact rollback.

options.text: We’ve never needed to roll back
options.why: ‘Never needed’ usually means ‘never tested’ — an untested rollback plan is a hope.

scenarios.title: Behavioral: ‘Tell me about an outage you handled’
scenarios.context: The SRE behavioral round. They want the war story — told like an SRE.

options.text: One with real user impact where your decisions mattered — stakes, your calls, the outcome
options.why: Impact + your decisions = gradable evidence of judgment under pressure.

options.text: The funniest outage, regardless of your role in it
options.why: Entertainment isn’t evidence; if you were a bystander, there’s nothing to score.

options.text: A story where everything went perfectly
options.why: Frictionless stories reveal nothing about how you handle pressure or ambiguity.

options.text: Someone else’s outage you heard about
options.why: Secondhand stories can’t demonstrate your behavior — interviewers score you, not your anecdotes.

steps.prompt: You made a wrong call mid-incident (restarted the wrong tier). How do you tell it?

options.text: Name it plainly: what you did, what it cost, what you changed in the runbook after
options.why: Owning mistakes with a systemic fix is the blameless-culture signal SRE teams hire for.

options.text: Leave it out — the story is cleaner without it
options.why: Sanitized stories read as fiction; the wrong turn is where the learning — and the score — lives.

options.text: Blame the misleading dashboard
options.why: Blame, even of a tool, fails the ownership test; the fix belongs to the system, including you.

options.text: Say you’d do everything the same again
options.why: No-learning answers signal no growth — the opposite of what the question probes.

steps.prompt: How do you close the story?

options.text: The lesson as a changed practice: ‘now our runbook has X, and it caught Y last month’
options.why: A lesson with evidence it stuck turns a story into proof of growth.

options.text: ‘And that’s why I’m great under pressure’
options.why: Self-praise conclusions sound hollow; let the evidence make the claim.

options.text: Trail off after the resolution
options.why: No landing wastes the story’s arc — the lesson is the point.

options.text: Ask if they’ve had similar outages
options.why: Deflecting at the close surrenders the final impression; land your lesson first.

mockTasks.q: Containers differ from VMs in that they:
choices: Share the host OS kernel instead of virtualizing hardware
mockTasks.explain: No guest kernel per container: faster startup, denser packing, but a shared kernel attack surface.

choices: Changing an object ID in a request accesses another user’s data — missing authorization check
mockTasks.explain: Authentication proves who you are; authorization must then prove you may touch this object.

mockTasks.q: Stating the brute force first is strong because:
choices: It shows honest complexity reasoning and gives a working fallback while you optimize
mockTasks.explain: A correct slow solution on the board beats a blank editor; optimization then has a baseline.

choices: 1 − SLO: the allowed failure rate, spent deliberately on releases and risk
mockTasks.explain: 99.9% SLO → 0.1% budget: reliability as a spendable resource balancing velocity and stability.

mockTasks.q: Promoting the same immutable artifact through environments ensures:
choices: What you tested is what you ship — no rebuild skew between staging and prod
mockTasks.explain: Rebuilding per environment invalidates testing; immutable artifacts preserve it.

mockTasks.q: Under shared responsibility, an open S3 bucket is:
choices: The customer’s fault — data access control is in the customer’s layer
mockTasks.explain: The provider secures the service; you configure who can read your objects.

mockTasks.q: The root fix for XSS is:
choices: Context-appropriate output encoding of untrusted data (+ CSP in depth)
mockTasks.explain: XSS is code/data confusion in the browser; encoding keeps untrusted data as data.

mockTasks.q: Speed reps should always include stating complexity aloud because:
choices: The interview grades the analysis as well as the code — rehearse both together
mockTasks.explain: Rehearsing code without narration trains half the interview.

mockTasks.q: An ML system design that only covers the model is weak because:
choices: Production value lives in data, serving, and monitoring — the model is one piece
mockTasks.explain: Most ML failures are systems failures: skew, drift, latency — not the algorithm.

mockTasks.q: Enforcing policy at plan time (vs after deploy) is better because:
choices: Violations are blocked before they exist — prevention beats detection
mockTasks.explain: Shift-left for governance: the bad change never reaches the cloud.

choices: Allowed/rejected IP traffic metadata — who tried to reach whom
mockTasks.explain: Flow logs are the packet-level audit trail for security-group and routing diagnosis.

mockTasks.q: Wireshark showing repeated TCP retransmissions indicates:
choices: Packet loss or an unresponsive peer — a network-path problem, not application logic
mockTasks.explain: Retransmits are the transport layer saying ‘my packets aren’t getting through.’

mockTasks.q: Labeling arrows with what flows matters because:
choices: Unlabeled arrows hide the data story — the labels are where the design lives
mockTasks.explain: Architecture is data in motion; unlabeled arrows are just boxes.

choices: Removing blame gets honest timelines — people report what really happened
mockTasks.explain: Honest data requires psychological safety; blame produces cover stories instead of root causes.

mockTasks.q: The primary defense against drift is:
choices: Everything through code + scheduled plan/detect cycles
mockTasks.explain: If all changes flow through IaC, reality can’t silently diverge.

mockTasks.q: VPC peering is preferred over public IPs for inter-VPC traffic because:
choices: Traffic stays on the private backbone — no internet exposure
mockTasks.explain: Private routing beats public routing for both security and latency.

blocks.body: **SLI** = measured ratio (good events / total). **SLO** = target on the SLI (99.9% / 30d). **Error budget** = 1 − SLO. **Burn rate** = budget consumption speed vs the SLO window.
Allowed failures = total requests × (1 − SLO). Consumed % = failed ÷ allowed × 100. 99.9% over 1M requests → 1,000 allowed failures. Exhausted budget → freeze risky releases.
Fast-burn: page (multiwindow, e.g. 1h + 5m at 14x). Slow-burn: ticket. Alert on **symptoms** (burn rate, golden signals), never on causes.
Latency, traffic, errors, saturation. **USE** for resources (Utilization, Saturation, Errors). **RED** for services (Rate, Errors, Duration).

**Pod** (smallest unit) → **Deployment** (replicas + rolling updates) → **Service** (stable DNS/LB) → **Ingress** (external HTTP routing). **ConfigMap/Secret** for config; never bake config into images.
**CrashLoopBackOff** — container can’t stay alive (bad cmd/config/probe). **ImagePullBackOff** — registry/auth. **OOMKilled** — limits vs reality. **Pending** — no schedulable node.

- `kubectl get pods` — what’s happening
- `kubectl describe` — events narrate
- `kubectl logs --previous` — why it died
- `kubectl top` — resource pressure
- `rollout history` — what changed

blocks.body: **IC**: decides, coordinates — doesn’t debug. **Comms**: status updates. **Scribe**: timeline. **SMEs**: debug.
Detect → respond (declare, assemble) → **mitigate first** → resolve → blameless postmortem. Mitigation before root cause, always.
One channel (#incident), every ~15 min even with ‘no update’, impact-first: who’s affected, what we’re doing, when’s next.
Blameless. Timeline, plural root causes (five whys with evidence), action items **with owners and dates**. The action items are the product.
Hypothesis → test → observe → update — **said out loud**. Time-box each hypothesis; narrate what each command tests.
DNS resolves? → TCP connects? → TLS handshakes? → HTTP responds? Each layer’s test isolates the fault.

answerBank.q: What is an SLO, and why does the error budget matter?
answerBank.a: An SLO is a target on a measured indicator — e.g. 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days. The error budget (1 − SLO) turns reliability into arithmetic: budget remaining means ship freely; budget exhausted means freeze risky changes. It replaces arguments about ‘reliable enough’ with a number both product and engineering agree on, and burn-rate alerting pages us only when the objective is actually at risk.

answerBank.q: Walk me through your incident response.
answerBank.a: Declare the incident and assume command — the IC coordinates, doesn’t debug. Open the bridge and #incident, assign comms and scribe. Mitigate first (rollback, shed load), understand second. Comms go out every ~15 minutes, impact-first. Afterward: blameless postmortem with a timeline, plural root causes from evidence, and action items with owners and dates — because the action items are the actual product.

answerBank.q: How would you design a canary deployment?
answerBank.a: Ship the new version to a small percentage first, with automated promotion gated on error-rate and latency comparisons against the baseline — and automated rollback on breach. I’d keep the previous immutable artifact one command away, make DB migrations backward-compatible via expand-contract, and rehearse the rollback. Canary bounds the blast radius: problems meet 1% of users before 100%.

answerBank.q: Latency just spiked. How do you troubleshoot it live?
answerBank.a: Hypothesis-driven and narrated: check the four golden signals to scope it (which service, which endpoints via RED), correlate with deploy annotations — ‘what changed?’ is the first question — then bisect: is it downstream, the data layer (slow queries, pool exhaustion), or resource saturation (USE)? Each command tests one hypothesis; I time-box and update out loud rather than guessing silently.

answerBank.q: Blue-green vs canary vs rolling — how do you choose?
answerBank.a: By blast-radius tolerance and cost. Blue-green: instant cutover and rollback, but double capacity. Canary: safest for risky user-facing changes — progressive exposure with metric gates. Rolling: simplest, slowest rollback. I’d default to canary for the user-facing API, and I always name the rollback story for whichever I pick — a strategy without a rollback plan is a hope.

answerBank.q: How would you secure a cloud account from scratch?
answerBank.a: Identity first: SSO federation, no long-lived keys, workload roles, least-privilege policies with no wildcards. Guardrails: SCPs blocking the dangerous actions, Config rules detective. Data: KMS encryption at rest, TLS everywhere, secrets in a manager — never in repos or images. Logging: CloudTrail on with an audit trail nobody can quietly disable. Then policy-as-code so the guardrails are compiler errors, not wiki pages.

answerBank.q: Tell me about an outage you handled.
answerBank.a: STAR with SRE texture: the stakes fast (what was down, who was affected), the investigation as hypotheses tested — including the wrong call I made and what it cost — and the landing as a changed practice: what went into the runbook and the evidence it stuck. I keep it blameless and systems-focused; the lesson with proof is the whole point of the story.
